title: Trump Booed, Mocked by Stewart After Crashing World Cup Trophy Ceremony
excerpt: The U.S. president drew loud jeers at MetLife Stadium and refused to leave the stage as Spain celebrated their second World Cup title, prompting a blistering response from The Daily Show host.
body:
• Trump was booed at MetLife Stadium during the World Cup final trophy ceremony, with crowd noise rising from 78 to 84 decibels according to the White House press pool report.
  • Jon Stewart devoted his Daily Show monologue to attacking Trump for lingering on stage during Spain's celebration, asking "What the f--- are you doing on the stage?"
  • FIFA and Spain's official accounts appeared to crop Trump out of celebration photos, while Argentina's Cristian Romero visibly bypassed a handshake with the president.
  • The incident has intensified calls for FIFA president Gianni Infantino to resign over his close association with Trump throughout the tournament.

President Donald Trump was met with sustained booing at MetLife Stadium on Sunday night after walking onto the field during the 2026 World Cup final trophy ceremony — and then refusing to leave. Jon Stewart devoted his Monday monologue on The Daily Show to eviscerating Trump's decision to linger on stage as Spain's players celebrated their 1-0 extra-time victory over Argentina, the crowning moment of a tournament already mired in political controversy.

A Night of High Drama On and Off the Pitch

The scene unfolded after a tense final that required 120 minutes to decide. Spain's Ferran Torres scored the only goal in the 106th minute, finishing off a headed pass from Nico Williams to secure Spain's second World Cup title and first since 2010. Argentina were reduced to 10 men late in regulation after midfielder Enzo Fernández received a second yellow card for a challenge on Pau Cubarsi, tilting the balance decisively.

Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez made 11 saves — a World Cup final record — but his side managed just two shots in 120 minutes, none on target. Spain fired 20 shots and dominated throughout, ending Argentina's bid to become the first repeat champions since Brazil in 1962. For 39-year-old Lionel Messi, it was likely his final World Cup match.

Trump arrived at the stadium aboard Marine One roughly 20 minutes before kickoff and was seated in a glassed-in VIP section alongside FIFA president Gianni Infantino, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney — the leaders of the three co-host nations. He received scattered boos when briefly shown on the stadium's video boards after the national anthem.

The full-throated jeering came later. When Trump and Infantino walked onto the pitch for the medal presentation, crowd noise jumped from 78 to 84 decibels, according to HuffPost White House reporter S.V. Dáte's pool report. "The president walked onto the field at 1826 to a sustained chorus of boos," Dáte wrote.

"Video showed Infantino physically attempting to usher the president away from the group — without success.</p> <blockquote class="pull-quote"><p>"What the f--- are you doing on the stage?"

"Video showed Infantino physically attempting to usher the president away from the group — without success.</p> <blockquote class="pull-quote"><p>"What the f--- are you doing on the stage?"

Stewart's Blistering Takedown

After presenting medals to both teams and handing Spain the trophy alongside Infantino, Trump remained on stage as the players prepared for their celebratory lift. Video showed Infantino physically attempting to usher the president away from the group — without success.

"What the f--- are you doing on the stage? Why must everything be tainted by the overinflated ego of Cankles Muldoon?"

— Jon Stewart, The Daily Show

Spain's official X account subsequently posted celebration photos that appeared to crop Trump out entirely. In one widely shared image, only the edge of his navy suit was visible in a corner. FIFA's official account similarly appeared to frame its shots to exclude the president.

Argentina defender Cristian Romero, the Tottenham center-back, added to the spectacle when he walked past Trump without shaking his hand during the medal presentation, greeting Infantino, Sheinbaum, and Carney but bypassing the U.S. president entirely. Spain's Borja Iglesias, who had previously said "I don't want to go to prison" about the prospect of meeting Trump, did shake his hand but avoided making eye contact.

Stewart also targeted a post-match interview in which Trump declared the event was "four times greater than any FIFA ever held." The host responded: "What's a FIFA? How do you hold a FIFA?" When Trump escalated his claim — "It's probably about five times, actually, they're telling me today" — Stewart fired back: "You know, they're telling you that because everyone around you lies to you, because you're a weirdo."

Mounting Pressure on Infantino

The fallout extends well beyond late-night comedy. U.S. Soccer vice president Nathán Goldberg Crenier published a scathing editorial in The Guardian accusing Infantino of making a "Faustian bargain" with Trump and leaving a "moral stain" on the tournament.

"No amount of revenue will ever erase the moral stain of blessing Trump's wars in the name of soccer."

— Nathán Goldberg Crenier, U.S. Soccer vice president

LaLiga president Javier Tebas went further, telling reporters that Infantino should resign after a decade at the helm. "In my opinion, yes, I think he has had his day," Tebas said, adding: "I don't know if silence or complicity is worse because those who are silent are perfectly aware of the damage that football is suffering."

The scrutiny comes after a tournament already marked by controversy, including Trump's personal intervention to suspend a red card issued to U.S. forward Folarin Balogun during the group stage — a move that appeared to contradict FIFA's own disciplinary bylaws.

What Comes Next

For Trump, the scene at MetLife Stadium was the latest in a pattern of hostile receptions at major sporting events during his second term, following loud booing at Game 3 of the NBA Finals at Madison Square Garden in June. The White House has not addressed the World Cup incident directly.

For FIFA, the pressure on Infantino shows no signs of easing. His close association with Trump, the bloated 48-team format, and now calls for further expansion to 64 teams for the 2030 tournament have united critics across the football world. Whether that translates into a genuine challenge to his leadership remains to be seen — but the images from Sunday night, including a world football body's own hurried attempt to crop the U.S. president out of victory photos, will be difficult to forget.
